passage: In the language of property, home and ownership have become almost interchangeable. To own the place one lives in is to 'have a home'; to rent is to be on the way to one, or to have failed to arrive. The equation is so familiar that it seems less a claim than a definition, and policies built on it, from subsidised mortgages to the sale of public housing to its tenants, present themselves not as choices among ways of housing people but as the extension of home itself to those who lack it.

Yet if one asks what people mean when they say that a place feels like home, the answers rarely mention title. They mention routines that have settled into the rooms, objects arranged by one's own hand, the confidence that one will be there next year, the freedom to decide who comes in, the ability to paint a wall or plant a window box or keep a dog. Home, in this sense, is less a thing one possesses than something one does, a practice of shaping a space and being shaped by it over time. And a practice of this kind needs two conditions: enough control over the space to shape it, and enough security of tenure to make the shaping worthwhile.

Neither condition is the same as ownership, though ownership has usually supplied both. A tenant on a twelve-month lease who may be asked to leave at short notice, who must seek permission to hang a picture, and whose rent can rise without limit, has good reason not to invest himself in his rooms; he is camping, however long he stays. But the cause of his condition is not that he rents. It is that his tenancy is short, revocable and hedged with prohibitions. Where tenancies are long, rents predictable and tenants free to alter their surroundings within reason, renters make homes much as owners do, while an owner whose mortgage payments consume most of his income, and who fears that a lost job means a lost house, may know the very precariousness that the equation reserves for tenants.

None of this means that ownership confers nothing distinctive. The owner can knock down a wall, not merely paint it; he can leave the house to his children; he answers to no landlord. A tenant, however secure, lives in a space whose final shape is decided by someone else. These are real goods, and it would be odd to deny that many people want them for good reasons. The objection is not to ownership but to the assumption that it is the only door into home, an assumption that directs public effort towards turning tenants into owners while leaving the conditions of tenancy, under which a large and often growing share of urban households live, largely untouched.

The cost of that assumption is not only sentimental. A household that expects to move at a landlord's word does not join the school committee, does not plant a tree it will not see grow, does not learn the names of neighbours it may lose within the year. Schools, associations and local shops all depend on residents who expect to stay long enough for their efforts to bear fruit. The practices through which people make a home are continuous with those through which they make a neighbourhood, so that insecurity inside the door becomes thinness of attachment outside it. To treat home as a matter of title is therefore to misunderstand not only what renters lack but what cities lose when they lack it.

passage: Trade statistics were designed for a world in which goods were made in one place and sold in another. A customs officer records the full value of a shipment as it crosses the border and attributes it to the country from which it was sent. When a product is made from start to finish in a single country, this convention is harmless. When it is assembled from parts made in a dozen, the convention produces a curious distortion: the country where the last screw is turned is credited with the entire value of the product, including the much larger share that was created elsewhere and merely passed through.

Consider a hypothetical tablet computer assembled in one country from a display made in a second, chips designed in a third and fabricated in a fourth, and software written in a fifth. When the finished tablet is shipped to a sixth country, the statistics record an export of its full factory price from the assembling country, though the work done there may account for only a small fraction of that price. The bilateral balance between the assembler and the buyer swells accordingly, while the suppliers of the costlier components, whose contribution travels unseen inside the assembler's shipment, appear in the bilateral figures as having sold nothing to the final market at all.

Statisticians have responded by trying to trace value added: to ask, for each product, how much of its value was created in each country, and to tally trade on that basis. The striking feature of the results is not that a country's overall position changes, for it largely does not. Its balance with the world as a whole is much the same however one counts, since the value of each imported component is recorded once as an import and again inside the export, and the two entries cancel. What changes is the map: the bilateral balances that attract political attention are redistributed, often substantially, from assemblers towards the countries that supply the most valuable parts.

This matters because bilateral balances are routinely read as a scorecard of who is gaining at whose expense, and policy is sometimes made on that reading. A tariff aimed at the country with which a large deficit is recorded may, on the value-added view, fall chiefly on workers who contributed a modest share of what was bought, while leaving untouched the countries that contributed the most. The value-added figures are not beyond dispute. They depend on tables of who buys inputs from whom that are compiled infrequently and filled out with estimates, and they cannot replace the gross figures that customs administrations need for their own purposes. But one need not regard them as precise to see that they expose a habit of reading the gross bilateral figures as though they measured something they were never built to measure.

passage: Governments that once judged their success almost entirely by output have lately begun to ask citizens a different question: all things considered, how satisfied are you with your life these days? The answers, usually given on a scale from zero to ten, are collected, averaged and compared across regions and years, and a rising average is increasingly cited as evidence that policy is working. The appeal of this approach is easy to understand. Income is at best a means to living well, and a measure that asks people directly about their lives seems to cut out the middleman.

Yet the question is less direct than it looks. To answer it, a respondent must do something quite unlike reporting a sensation. She must call to mind her life as a whole, choose the standards by which it is to be judged, and compare the one with the other. The number she gives is therefore an evaluation, and evaluations depend on the standards brought to them. Two people whose days contain the same mixture of pleasure, worry and boredom may give very different scores because one expects more from life than the other. A person who has learned to expect little can report contentment with circumstances that would dismay a neighbour, and a population whose expectations rise quickly can report falling satisfaction even as its conditions improve.

None of this makes the surveys worthless. Evaluations matter in their own right: how people judge their lives shapes what they choose, whom they blame and whether they think change is possible. The scores also move in ways we would expect, dropping when people lose their jobs or fall seriously ill. The error lies not in collecting the numbers but in treating them as a complete reading of how well people are living. A measure of judgement is not a measure of experience, and neither is it a measure of whether a life contains the goods, such as health, friendship and freedom, that most traditions of thought have held to be worth having whatever one happens to feel about them.

A sensible policy, then, would treat satisfaction scores as one instrument among several, read alongside measures of how people actually spend and feel their days and of what they are really able to do. Used alone, the scores reward whatever lowers expectations as readily as whatever improves lives, and a government that steered by them alone could succeed by teaching its citizens to want less.

passage: The quarrel between those who lay down rules for English and those who merely record how it is spoken is usually staged as a contest between snobbery and science. On one side stand the guardians of usage, who object to split infinitives and sentence-final prepositions and who regard each new sense of an old word as a small act of vandalism. On the other stand the linguists, who point out that many of the rules are of recent and dubious origin, that admired writers have broken them for centuries, and that a grammar describing what speakers actually do is the only kind that deserves the name. Put this way, the linguists win easily, and in the universities, at least, they have been winning for a long time.

Yet the victory is less complete than it appears, because it rests on a confusion about what a rule of usage is. The linguist is right that no rule of this kind is a law of the language in the way that, say, the order of article and noun is: speakers who break it are still perfectly understood, and they are still speaking English. But it does not follow that such rules are mere prejudice. Beliefs about correctness are themselves part of the linguistic behaviour of a community. A speaker who avoids a construction in a job application while using it freely at home is not confused; she is responding accurately to a social fact, namely that certain readers will judge her by it. A descriptive grammar that ignored such judgements would be describing an imaginary community.

What the prescriptivist gets wrong is not the existence of the rules but their source. The traditional defence appeals to logic, or to the example of Latin, or to a clarity the condemned construction supposedly lacks. These appeals rarely survive inspection. The objection to splitting an infinitive, for instance, makes some sense in a language where the infinitive is a single word and cannot be split, and very little in one where it is two. The real authority of such a rule is conventional: it binds because enough educated readers expect it to be observed, and for no deeper reason.

Seeing the rules as conventions of a register, rather than as laws or as prejudices, changes the question we should ask about them. It is no longer whether a usage is correct in some absolute sense, but whether a given convention earns its keep: whether it marks a distinction readers find useful, or merely sets a test that excludes those who were never taught it. Some conventions pass that test; many fail it. The point is that they can be judged, and that judging them is neither the snob's work nor the scientist's alone.

passage: The idea of a keystone species borrows its name from architecture. In an arch, the keystone is the wedge at the top that holds the other stones in place; remove it, and the structure falls. Applied to ecosystems, the term picks out species whose effect on their community is far larger than their abundance would suggest, so that their loss sets off changes that ripple through many other species. A predator that keeps a grazer in check, allowing plants to flourish, is the classic case, and the concept has proved enormously useful in persuading the public and governments that the fate of a single species can matter to a whole landscape.

The vividness of the metaphor, however, carries assumptions that ecology does not always support. An arch has one keystone, and its role is fixed by the geometry of the structure. Ecological communities are not like this. The same species may have a dominant influence in one place and a minor one in another, depending on what else lives there, on the climate and on the history of the site. A predator that controls its prey on a rocky shore where that prey has few other enemies may matter much less where the prey is also eaten by several other animals. Keystone status, in other words, is a property of a relationship in a particular setting, not a fixed attribute of a species.

The metaphor also invites a search for the one species that holds everything together, when in many communities influence is spread across several species, each of moderate importance, whose combined effects are what keep the system stable. A conservation strategy built around identifying and protecting keystones may then direct attention to a few dramatic interactions and neglect the diffuse ones, which are harder to demonstrate but not necessarily less important. The absence of a striking keystone in a community does not show that its members are interchangeable.

None of this means the concept should be discarded. Some species really do have outsized and well-documented effects, and naming them helps in arguing for their protection. The danger lies in treating the label as a discovery about a species' nature rather than a finding about a particular system, and in assuming that where no keystone has been identified, no species is indispensable. The architectural image is best used as what it is, a way of making one kind of ecological fact memorable, and not as a model of how communities are generally built.

passage: Every entrenched constitution invites an awkward question. If a majority of citizens today wishes to change some arrangement, why should it be prevented from doing so by rules that were drafted generations ago by people who are now dead, and who could not have imagined the conditions under which their successors live? A requirement that amendments win two-thirds of the legislature, or the approval of most regions, looks from this angle like a device for letting the past outvote the present. The objection has a democratic edge that is hard to dismiss: it asks by what right one generation sets the terms on which another must govern itself. Nor is it answered by praising the wisdom of the framers, since wisdom about one century is no warrant for authority over the next.

The most familiar answer appeals to self-binding. Just as a sailor who knows he will be tempted by a dangerous song may order his crew to tie him to the mast and ignore his later pleas, a people may bind itself in a calm moment against the passions it expects to feel in an agitated one. Entrenchment, on this account, is not the past overruling the present but the present protecting itself from its own worst impulses. The image is attractive, but it does not fit the case. The sailor binds himself, and the man who later strains at the ropes is the same man who gave the order. A constitution binds people who were not present when it was adopted and who gave no order at all. To call this self-binding is to assume precisely the continuity of the collective self that the objection calls into question.

A better defence starts from a different picture of what entrenchment does. Amendment rules do not, in practice, pit the living against the dead, because the dead cast no votes. What such rules do is set the terms on which living citizens must settle disagreements among themselves. When an amendment fails for want of a supermajority, it is defeated not by its framers but by a present minority large enough to block it. The requirement thus protects groups that might otherwise be outvoted on matters basic to their standing, and it encourages proposals that can attract support beyond a single faction. The protection is not merely theoretical: a group that knows it can block changes to its basic standing has less reason to fear the ordinary swings of electoral fortune, and more reason to accept defeat on everything else. Seen this way, the hand that restrains the majority is a living hand, and the real question is whether present minorities deserve such a veto, not whether the past deserves obedience.

This reframing does not make the original worry vanish. It succeeds only where amendment is demanding but genuinely possible. A constitution whose amendment procedure is so onerous that no change has been achieved in living memory, or which declares certain provisions unamendable altogether, really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after; there, no present coalition, however broad, can alter the text. The objection from the dead hand is therefore best understood not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes. Between a constitution that any passing majority may rewrite and one that no one can, the useful argument concerns how much agreement change should require, and that is a question each generation is entitled to keep asking.

passage: In the last two decades the walkable neighbourhood has become one of the few planning ideals on which almost everyone claims to agree, and with agreement has come measurement. Composite indices now rate districts by the number of shops, schools and stops within a short radius, the density of street intersections and the share of homes near public transport. Estate agents quote such figures; municipal plans set targets for raising them. It would be churlish to deny the good these indices have done. They gave walking, long treated as what people did when they could not drive, a place in the arithmetic of planning, and they made visible how many districts had been designed as if nobody would ever arrive on foot.

Yet what the indices measure is proximity, and proximity is not the same as walkability. A street can lie within five minutes of a pharmacy, a school and a bus stop and still be miserable to walk along: a narrow pavement beside four lanes of fast traffic, no shade under a summer sun, the blank walls of parking structures on either side, crossings that demand a long detour. Two districts with identical scores can therefore offer entirely different experiences, and the index has no way of registering the difference, because it counts what lies at the end of the walk and ignores the walk itself.

This blindness is not accidental; it reflects an assumption that walking is chiefly a means of reaching places. For many people it is that, but it is also something more: the way a child learns a neighbourhood, the way an elderly resident keeps in contact with the world, the occasion for the chance encounters on which local life depends. These goods are produced en route, by the quality of the street, its pace, its frontages, its benches and its shade, not by the count of destinations. A measure built around destinations will systematically undervalue them.

The danger is sharpest when the index ceases to be a description and becomes a target. A city told to raise its score can do so cheaply by permitting a few more shops near existing homes, while the hostile road that separates residents from those shops remains untouched. The number improves; the walk does not. None of this argues for abandoning measurement. It argues for remembering what the measurement leaves out, and for treating a high score as the beginning of an inquiry into a street rather than its conclusion.

passage: Long before there were central banks, people understood that a ruler who clipped the edges of coins, or mixed base metal into silver, was taking a share of his subjects' wealth without asking them. The modern version of the idea holds that a government which finances its spending by creating money imposes an inflation tax on everyone who holds that money. No law is passed and no collector calls; the price of bread simply rises, and the real value of the cash in people's pockets falls in proportion. In one respect the analogy with taxation is exact: resources move from the public to the issuer of money, who has spent the new money before its effect on prices is felt.

Critics of this practice argue that it is worse than ordinary taxation precisely because it is hidden: a tax on incomes must be proposed, debated and voted upon; an inflation tax requires only that the issuing authority do nothing to stop it. It also tends to fall heavily on those least able to protect themselves, such as households that keep their savings in cash or depend on incomes fixed in money terms, while it benefits anyone whose debts shrink in real value as prices rise. Among the largest such debtors, of course, is often the state itself.

The analogy misleads, however, when it is pressed too far. A tax is a deliberate choice, whereas much inflation arises from events that no government chose, such as a failed harvest, a war in a distant region or a sudden jump in the price of fuel. Moreover, where most money takes the form of bank deposits that pay interest, and where that interest rises when inflation rises, the revenue a state gains from mild inflation is modest. To describe every increase in prices as a tax is to attribute intention and gain in cases where there may be neither.

What the old idea gets right is the question it trains us to ask: who gains? When inflation is high and persistent and the state is a heavy debtor, the answer frequently points to the treasury, and the language of taxation is then not rhetoric but accurate description. When inflation is mild, or arrives from abroad through the price of imports, the same language obscures more than it reveals. The concept of an inflation tax is best treated as a tool of diagnosis rather than as a verdict reached in advance.

passage: The secret ballot is now so taken for granted that it is easy to forget how recent it is and how fiercely it was once opposed. For much of the nineteenth century, in many countries, voters declared their choices aloud or on papers that others could see, and the reform that replaced this practice was resisted not only by those who profited from intimidation. A respectable strand of liberal opinion held that the vote was a public trust, exercised on behalf of the whole community, and that a trust ought to be discharged in public. A man who knew that his neighbours would see his vote, the argument ran, would be ashamed to cast it for a selfish reason.

The argument has a certain nobility, and it rests on a real insight: people do behave differently when they are observed. Its error lies in assuming that the observer will be the voter's conscience. In practice the people most interested in how a tenant, a labourer or a clerk had voted were the landlord, the employer and the local party agent, and the pressure they applied had little to do with the public good. Publicity did not make votes more responsible; it made them more obedient.

The less obvious virtue of secrecy is that it disarms bribery as well as intimidation. Buying a vote is a kind of contract, and a contract is worthless if one party cannot check whether the other has kept it. Once no one can verify how a ballot was marked, the buyer who pays in advance cannot know whether he has bought anything, and the seller can take the money and vote as he pleases. Secrecy, in other words, works less by appealing to the voter's virtue than by making a certain kind of corruption unenforceable. This also explains why secrecy has to be a duty and not merely a right. If voters could choose to reveal their ballots, those under pressure could be required to prove their compliance, and the protection would collapse for exactly the people who need it most.

That point matters more now than it once did. A ballot marked at home, at a kitchen table, can be watched by a domineering relative; a ballot photographed in a booth with a telephone can be shown to whoever demands proof. Neither practice is sinister in itself, and both make voting easier for many people. But they reopen the gap that secrecy was designed to close, and they suggest that the privacy of the vote is not a natural condition of democratic life but an arrangement that has to be maintained, and occasionally rebuilt, as the means of voting change.

passage: Among the people who first tried to build thinking machines, a surprise emerged that has never quite been absorbed. The tasks that seemed to demand the most intelligence, such as proving theorems, playing chess or solving problems in algebra, turned out to be comparatively tractable for computers, while tasks that any small child performs without effort, such as recognising a face across a room, picking up an unfamiliar object or walking over uneven ground, proved stubbornly hard. The observation is often associated with the roboticist Hans Moravec, and it is usually called a paradox. Whether it deserves the name depends on what we took difficulty to be in the first place.

The most common explanation is evolutionary. Seeing, grasping and moving have been refined over hundreds of millions of years of animal life, and the machinery that performs them is vast, ancient and almost entirely hidden from awareness. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is a recent arrival, practised deliberately and with effort. We notice the effort and conclude that reasoning is hard; we notice nothing when we recognise a friend's face, and conclude that perception is easy. On this account the paradox is an artefact of introspection: our sense of difficulty tracks how much of a skill reaches consciousness, not how much computation it requires.

This explanation is persuasive, but it should not be stretched into the claim that every skill we find effortless is computationally deep, or that every skill we find laborious is shallow. Some effortless skills may be easy for machines too, and some laborious ones, like long division, are trivial for any pocket calculator while others remain hard. The evolutionary story explains a general tendency; it does not supply a rule. Nor has the gap stood still. Machines have become far better at recognising images and speech than early researchers expected, though a robot that can fold an unfamiliar garment or clear an untidy table remains much harder to build than a program that plays chess at a master's level.

The deeper lesson concerns our idea of intelligence itself. For a long time intelligence was identified with the activities that educated adults found hardest and prized most: calculation, logic, formal games. The paradox suggests that this identification was parochial. What humans find hard is a measure of human limitations, not a measure of how much intelligence a task needs, and the competences we share with other animals may contain more of what is difficult about minds than the competences that distinguish us. A cat crossing a cluttered shelf without disturbing anything is solving problems that our best machines still find formidable, and it would be odd to call that achievement unintelligent merely because no cat could sit an examination.

passage: Political parties have few admirers. It is a commonplace of political commentary that they are distrusted, and reformers of every persuasion have proposed ways of loosening their grip: independent candidates, direct votes on policy, primaries open to any voter who cares to take part. The suspicion is understandable. Parties reward loyalty over judgement, they paper over disagreements in order to win, and their leaders sometimes seem more interested in the survival of the organisation than in the purposes it was founded to serve.

Yet much of what makes democratic government workable is done by parties, and done so routinely that it goes unnoticed. A modern electorate contains millions of people with conflicting interests. Someone has to assemble those interests into a programme coherent enough to be offered, defended and, if elected, attempted; someone has to recruit and test the people who will hold office; and someone has to give voters a simple way of knowing what a candidate broadly stands for without studying the record of each individual. Parties do all three. Most importantly, they make accountability possible. A government formed by a party can be judged as a team at the next election, whereas a legislature of independents, each with a private bargain to defend, offers voters no one in particular to reward or punish.

This is why some reforms intended to democratise parties have had awkward consequences. When candidates are chosen in primaries open to anyone, the party organisation loses much of its ability to screen out those who would damage it, and the candidates who win are often those with the most intense supporters rather than those with the broadest appeal. When membership dwindles, the organisation does not disappear; it becomes a smaller circle of professionals and funders, less rooted in local life and more remote from the voters it claims to represent. Weakening the party, in other words, does not necessarily hand power to citizens. It may hand it instead to whoever is able to organise without one: wealthy individuals, single-issue lobbies, the personal following of a celebrity.

None of this makes parties virtuous. A party that faces no serious competition will serve itself, and the defenders of party government have sometimes mistaken the indispensability of parties for their innocence. The argument here is a narrower one. It is that the familiar complaints about parties are complaints about particular parties behaving badly, and that the cure for bad parties is better ones, more open to their members and more seriously contested, rather than a politics that tries to do without them altogether.

passage: Two attitudes to the character of the speaker run through the study of persuasion, and they are hard to reconcile. The first, familiar from introductory logic, holds that an argument stands or falls on its own terms. Who makes it is irrelevant; to reject a claim because of the person advancing it is to commit a fallacy, and to accept a claim because of the person is the same error in a friendlier mood. The second attitude is older. Aristotle counted the character of the speaker among the means of persuasion, alongside appeals to the emotions of the audience and to the argument itself, and he did not present it as a regrettable weakness of listeners. A speaker who seems sensible, honest and well disposed towards the audience is, on this view, more worthy of belief, and an audience is right to take that into account.

The logician's attitude is correct for a particular situation: one in which the listener can examine the argument fully. A proof in geometry is no better for coming from a famous mathematician. But most of the claims on which people must act are not like proofs. A patient cannot check a diagnosis, a juror cannot repeat the forensic analysis, and a citizen cannot audit the statistics behind a policy. In such cases the listener is not choosing between evaluating the argument and evaluating the speaker; the argument is largely out of reach, and the speaker's record, competence and incentives are the best evidence available. To attend to them is not a lapse in reasoning but reasoning under a division of intellectual labour that no one can escape.

If this rehabilitates the appeal to character, it also shows where that appeal goes wrong. Credibility is earned in a domain. The physician's record is evidence about diagnoses, not about tax policy, and the honesty of a popular broadcaster is evidence that he reports what he believes, not that what he believes is true. Much modern persuasion works by carrying trust from the place where it was earned to a place where it has no bearing: the athlete who recommends an investment, the scientist who pronounces on matters far from her field. The listener who accepts such claims is not wrong to rely on character in general; she is wrong about which character she is relying on.

The two attitudes, then, are less opposed than they first appear. The logician is right that character cannot make a bad argument good, and the rhetorician is right that, where arguments cannot be inspected, character is often all a listener has to go on. What a careful audience needs is neither a rule against attending to the speaker nor a habit of trusting the likeable, but the narrower discipline of asking what, exactly, the speaker's credibility is credibility about.

passage: Few school subjects have lost their defenders as quickly as handwriting. When most adult writing passes through a keyboard or a touchscreen, the hours once devoted to forming letters on lined paper can look like a ritual preserved out of institutional habit rather than educational necessity. Why, the argument runs, should a child labour over the loops of a joined script that she will rarely use after leaving school, when the same time could be given to typing, programming or simply reading more widely? The objection has the considerable appeal of common sense, and part of it is right. But it rests on a narrow idea of what handwriting lessons were ever for.

The narrow idea treats handwriting as a delivery system, a way of getting words from a head onto a surface, and judged by that standard alone it has plainly been outpaced. Yet for a young child, forming a letter by hand is also a way of learning the letter. To write a b rather than a d, the child must attend to direction, proportion and the small differences that distinguish one shape from its neighbours, and that sustained attention seems to help fix the shapes in memory in a way that pressing a key does not. A keyboard presents every letter ready-made; the hand has to build each one. Several researchers have suggested that this building is part of how early readers come to recognise letters at all, though the evidence is still being argued over and is far from settled.

There is a second, quieter benefit, which concerns older students rather than beginners. Students who take notes by hand cannot transcribe a lecture word for word, because the hand is too slow. They are forced to choose, compress and rephrase, and that compression is itself a kind of thinking, an early and private interpretation of what the lecturer actually argued. The student with a laptop can capture far more, and may understand far less, since verbatim copying can proceed without the words ever being weighed. The slowness that makes handwriting look obsolete is, in this setting, precisely its use.

None of this is an argument for preserving every feature of the old curriculum. The insistence on one elegant joined style, and the marks lost for an untidy loop, had more to do with the manners of an earlier age than with learning, and they can be abandoned without much loss. Nor should typing be neglected in the name of tradition; children need both. The case for handwriting, properly made, is modest: not that it is beautiful or traditional, but that the hand teaches the eye and slows the mind in ways that are useful precisely because they are inefficient. A curriculum that drops it to save time may find that it has saved the wrong thing.

passage: Few scientific failures are held against a discipline as often as seismology's inability to say when the next large earthquake will strike. The public imagines that a sufficiently clever instrument, placed in the right fault zone, ought eventually to detect a warning sign, much as a barometer falls before a storm. Over the past century researchers have pursued many such signs, from changes in groundwater levels and gas emissions to swarms of small tremors and odd animal behaviour. Each has, at one time or another, appeared to precede a particular earthquake, and each has failed when tested against the many earthquakes that came without it and the many apparent warnings that were followed by nothing.

It is worth separating two activities that ordinary speech runs together. A prediction, in the sense the public wants, names a place, a magnitude and a narrow window of time: a strong earthquake near this town within the next week. A forecast states a probability over a longer period: a given chance of shaking above some level in this region within the next thirty years. The first remains beyond reach, and many seismologists suspect it may stay there, because whether a small rupture grows into a large one seems to depend on conditions deep in the crust that no instrument can survey in detail. The second is routine, and it is far from useless.

Forecasts are what building codes are written from. When engineers decide how strongly a hospital must be braced, or which soils are too loose to build on, they are acting on probabilities of exactly this kind. A city that has absorbed its long-term hazard into the way it builds has, in effect, already received the most valuable warning seismology can give, though nobody experiences it as a warning, since it arrives years before the event and asks for money rather than flight.

The objection that a probability is too vague to act on mistakes the kind of decision at stake. Few people would evacuate a city on the strength of a one-in-twenty chance spread over three decades, and nobody should. But a decision about whether to reinforce a school is not a decision about this week; it is a decision about the lifetime of a building, and over that lifetime a one-in-twenty chance is large. This does not mean that the search for warning signs should be abandoned, since a reliable one would save lives that codes cannot. It means that the discipline should not be judged by its failure at a task it may never accomplish while its success at a quieter task goes unremarked.

passage: The picture of the author that most readers carry is a picture of solitude: one person, one desk, one manuscript that emerges complete and is then merely printed. Publishing reinforces the picture at every step. The author's name alone goes on the cover, the author gives the interviews and accepts the prizes, and the acknowledgements page, where the other contributors are thanked, is the page readers most reliably skip. Yet anyone who has watched a book being made knows that the finished text is rarely the text the author first submitted.

Between those two texts stands, among others, the editor. At the broadest level, an editor may tell an author that the book begins in the wrong place, that a character is doing no work, or that the argument of a long middle section has already been made in its first ten pages. At the finest level, an editor queries a word, a comma, the order of two clauses. Much of this advice is accepted, some of it is fought over and some is refused; but the book that reaches the reader has been shaped by all three outcomes, since even a rejected suggestion can force an author to articulate why a passage must stay. The work is deliberately invisible. A good edit, like good stage lighting, is meant to pass unnoticed, and editors who want their contribution celebrated are generally thought to have misunderstood the job.

One tempting response is to declare that editors are secret co-authors and that the solitary author is a fraud. This overcorrects. In most cases the author supplies the material, the voice and the governing intention, and the editor works on what the author has made rather than making it; the relation resembles that between a performer and an exacting coach more than that between two composers. There are exceptions, cases in which an editor's cuts and rewritings have been so extensive that the question of whose book it is becomes genuinely difficult to answer, but they are exceptions precisely because they unsettle us.

The real lesson concerns how we assign credit rather than who deserves the most of it. Our habits treat authorship as an all-or-nothing property, possessed entirely by one person, when the making of most books is a graded collaboration in which contributions differ in kind as well as in size. Recognising this would not diminish authors. It would make it easier to see what they actually do, which is not to produce text from nothing but to direct a process that others help to carry out, and to bear responsibility for the result.

passage: Few natural experiments in linguistics are cited as often as the birth of a new sign language. Where deaf people who have had no shared language are brought together, at a newly founded school, say, or in a village where hereditary deafness is common, they do not remain without one for long. A system of signs takes shape among them, and within a few decades it has acquired the apparatus of a full language: consistent word order, ways of marking who did what to whom, devices for referring back to something already mentioned. The case is regularly offered as decisive evidence that the capacity for grammar is built into the human mind and needs only an occasion to express itself.

The evidence is real, but it supports a more interesting conclusion than the one usually drawn from it. A deaf child raised among hearing people who do not sign will typically invent gestures to communicate with her family, and these home signs show some structure of their own: distinct gestures for actions and for things, and a tendency to place them in a regular order. What they do not become, however long the child uses them, is a full language. The leap appears only where there are many signers, and it appears in stages. The first cohort, who created the system as adolescents or adults, typically use it with more variation and less regularity than the children who learn it from them; and it is those children, receiving a still untidy system and reproducing it more consistently than they found it, who drive it towards full grammatical form.

If grammar were simply waiting inside each mind for an occasion, the solitary home signer would have occasion enough. She has a lifetime of need, a willing family and an intact brain. What she lacks is other people who share her system and, above all, a younger generation to learn it from her. The emergence of a sign language thus looks less like the unveiling of a finished structure than like a process distributed across minds and generations, in which individual predispositions are amplified by repeated transmission until regularities that were faint in any single user become fixed in the community.

This is not to deny that the mind brings a great deal to the task. The speed of the process, a matter of decades rather than centuries, and the resemblance between the regularities that emerge and those found in long-established languages both point to strong biases in how children learn. But the case tells against the picture of language as an organ that grows in isolation, as surely as it tells against the picture of language as a mere convention on which people agree. A language turns out to need both a particular kind of learner and a particular kind of crowd.

passage: When the sea threatens a coastal town, the first response is almost always to defend it. Walls are raised, beaches are replenished with sand pumped from offshore, and the line between land and water is held where it has always been. To propose instead that some places should be gradually abandoned sounds like defeatism, a confession that the town has been given up for lost. Yet the choice is rarely between holding the line and surrendering it. More often it is between retreat that is planned and retreat that is forced.

Defences are not permanent solutions but commitments that grow. A wall built to withstand the storms of today must be raised as the sea rises, and every raising protects more property that was built because the previous wall made it seem safe. Each round of investment makes the next one harder to refuse, since abandoning the wall would now mean abandoning more. Engineers can usually design a higher barrier; the deeper difficulty is that the community sheltering behind it has, by then, organised its entire economic life around the expectation that the barrier will hold. In low-lying places the expense eventually outruns what the community can pay, and the decision to leave is then made not by a council in calm weather but by the storm that finally breaks through.

Retreat imposed in that way is the worst version of a policy that might have been tolerable. Households leave in a rush, with property that has lost its value overnight, and they scatter wherever they can find housing, so that the neighbourhood that made the place worth defending dissolves. Planned retreat, by contrast, can be slow. A town can stop permitting new building in the most exposed areas, offer to buy homes when owners choose to sell, and move a school or a clinic inland when it would have needed rebuilding anyway. Spread over decades, such steps let a community move as a community.

None of this means that every shore should be abandoned. Some coasts carry so much population and infrastructure that defending them is plainly worth the cost, and in poor places the money for orderly relocation is often lacking. Nor can retreat simply be ordered from above; people who have lived beside the water for generations have reasons for staying that no compensation formula captures, and a plan that ignores them will fail. The argument is narrower: retreat belongs among the options from the start, weighed openly alongside walls, rather than held back as an admission of failure until it can no longer be chosen at all.

options.C: each raising of a wall makes it stronger, so engineers become more confident that it will hold against future storms.
options.D: the cost of each new round of wall-building falls as the town's builders gain experience with the same structure.

passage: Discussions of nationality law often begin from a tidy contrast. Under the principle of soil, a child born within the territory of a state becomes its citizen; under the principle of descent, citizenship passes from parent to child wherever the child is born. The first is commonly described as civic and open, since it admits anyone born on the land regardless of ancestry; the second as ethnic and closed, since it ties membership to bloodline. The contrast is useful as a first approximation, but as a guide to which societies are more welcoming it is close to misleading.

Consider why states adopted the soil rule in the first place. Where governments needed to populate large territories and to secure soldiers and taxpayers, it was convenient to claim the children of newcomers automatically, whatever their parents' wishes or origins. The rule expressed less a generous conception of belonging than an interest in numbers. Conversely, the descent rule has served countries with large populations abroad, allowing the children of emigrants to retain a connection to a homeland they may visit only occasionally. Neither motive is obviously more liberal than the other, and the same rule can serve quite different ends depending on who adopts it and why.

More importantly, the rule that governs birth is only one part of a citizenship regime, and often not the part that matters most. A state that follows the descent principle but allows long-term residents to naturalise after a few years, and extends citizenship to children who have grown up and been schooled in the country, may be far easier to join than a state that follows the soil principle but makes naturalisation slow, costly and uncertain for adults. The second state includes every child born on its territory and keeps their parents waiting at the door indefinitely. A single household may then contain citizens and foreigners under one roof, divided by nothing more than the place where each member happened to be born.

None of this means the choice of birth rule is unimportant. The soil principle does guarantee something valuable: no one born in the territory can be left, by the mere fact of birth, a permanent outsider in the only country he has known, and states without it have sometimes produced generations of residents with no secure status. But that guarantee is better understood as one protection among several than as the defining mark of an open society. The question worth asking of any nationality law is not which principle it starts from, but how readily it turns people who have made their lives in a country into its members.

passage: Every wave of labour-saving machinery revives an old piece of arithmetic. If a factory needs a fixed quantity of work done, and a new machine does a third of it, then a third of the workers must go. Extend the sum across a whole economy and the conclusion seems inescapable: the more productive we become, the fewer of us will be needed. Economists have a name for the premise hidden in this calculation. They call it the lump of labour fallacy, the assumption that there is a set amount of work to be shared out, so that any work done by a machine, a newcomer or a pensioner who stays on is necessarily work taken from someone else.

The premise fails because the quantity of work is not fixed; it depends on what people want and can afford. When a machine makes cloth cheaper, households that once owned two shirts buy five, and the money they no longer spend on clothing goes on furniture, travel or schooling, each of which employs someone. The jobs created in this way are rarely the jobs that were lost, and they often appear in places and trades that nobody at the time thought to connect with the original invention. That is precisely why the destruction is so visible and the creation so easy to overlook. A closed mill is a single event with an address; the thousand small expansions that follow are scattered across an economy and are reported, if at all, as ordinary growth.

The same error appears in proposals that look generous. Schemes to push older workers into early retirement so that the young can find work, or to cap weekly hours so that employment is spread more thinly, assume that the jobs given up by one group pass intact to another. There is little reason to expect this. A worker who retires early also stops earning and spending at the old rate, and a firm that loses an experienced employee may simply produce less rather than hire a novice to take her place.

None of this means that the anxiety is foolish. The fallacy concerns the total amount of work, not its distribution, and a correct argument about totals is cold comfort to a fifty-year-old weaver whose skills no longer have a buyer. Transitions can take a generation, and the people who bear their cost are seldom the people who collect the gains. The proper conclusion is narrower than either side usually admits: technology does not abolish work in aggregate, but it can ruin particular lives and places, and policy ought to be judged by what it does for them rather than by whether it rescues a fixed stock of jobs that never existed.

passage: Few technical metaphors have succeeded as completely as the cloud. To store files 'in the cloud' is to imagine them floating somewhere overhead, available from anywhere, belonging to no place in particular and weighing nothing at all. The image is not simply wrong; from the point of view of a user, it describes the experience rather well. A photograph taken on a phone appears on a laptop moments later, and the user neither knows nor needs to know where it has been in between. Yet the metaphor has migrated from describing an experience to shaping how whole societies think about a vast industrial system, and in that second role it misleads.

What sits behind the cloud is emphatically material. It consists of large buildings filled with servers, which consume great quantities of electricity and must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies; of cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines; of particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground. Each of these is somewhere, and being somewhere means being subject to the laws of a particular state, to the weather and geology of a particular region, and to the politics of the towns asked to host the buildings and supply their power. A data centre can strain a local grid or compete with farms for water, and a damaged cable can slow communication across a region.

The metaphor makes all of this hard to see. A cloud has no address, so questions about which country's courts can demand access to stored data come to seem technical rather than political. A cloud uses nothing, so the energy cost of keeping old files indefinitely available is easy to forget. And a cloud is diffuse, which suggests resilience, whereas in practice a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward with surprising speed.

Defenders of the metaphor might point out that hiding complexity is precisely what good computing does. Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message, and abstractions of this kind are why ordinary people can use powerful systems at all. That is true, but it confuses two audiences. Abstraction is a gift to the user at the moment of use; it becomes a liability when it is carried over into the deliberations of citizens, regulators and planners, whose task is precisely to decide where the buildings go, who supplies their power and whose laws govern what they hold. For them, the useful question is not where the cloud is but how it came to seem to be nowhere.

options.B: water drawn from local supplies to keep buildings full of servers cool.
options.C: sites chosen because they offer cheap power or favourable taxes.
options.D: satellites that relay stored data between continents when undersea links fail.
